content.text: Graphs are one of the most powerful tools in physics. They allow us to visualise motion, identify patterns, and extract quantitative information that would be difficult to see from numbers alone. A
(sometimes called a position-time graph) plots the distance or position of an object on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis.

By reading and interpreting distance-time graphs, you can determine whether an object is stationary, moving at constant speed, or changing speed — all without needing equations. In this lesson, we will learn how to plot, read, and interpret distance-time graphs, and we will develop the skill of calculating speed from the gradient of the graph.

Time is always the independent variable (placed on the x-axis), and distance is the dependent variable (placed on the y-axis).
The graph shows how an object's distance from a reference point changes as time progresses.

"A downward slope means the object is decelerating."
On a distance-time graph, the line never slopes downward because distance can only increase or stay the same (you cannot 'un-travel' a distance). A downward slope on a
graph means the object is returning to the starting point, not necessarily decelerating.
"The height of the graph tells you the speed."
The height (y-value) tells you the distance from the starting point, not the speed. The
"A straight line always means the object is moving."
straight line means the object is stationary. Only a
A steeper line means faster, not further. An object might be closer but moving faster than another object that is further away but moving slowly.
"A curve on a distance-time graph means the object is moving in a curve."
The curve on the graph represents changing speed, not a curved path. The object could be moving in a straight line while accelerating.
"You can read acceleration directly from a distance-time graph."
You cannot. Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, not a distance-time graph. From a distance-time graph, you can only determine speed.
Lines crossing on a distance-time graph mean the objects are at the same distance from the reference point at that time. They only meet if they are on the same path.
